title: What is OpenID Connect (OIDC) — a layer ON TOP of OAuth2 that adds AUTHENTICATION (who is the user) via an ID token (a JWT with user info like name, email, picture)?
shortTitle: OpenID Connect (OIDC) — Authentication Layer on Top of OAuth2

s1_definition.profdef: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer built on top of OAuth2 that adds standardized authentication — telling the client who the user is — whereas plain OAuth2 only handles authorization. OIDC introduces the ID token, a signed JWT containing identity claims such as sub, name, email, and picture, issued by the Authorization Server (acting as an OpenID Provider). The client validates the ID token to establish the user's identity, while still receiving an OAuth2 access token for calling APIs. OIDC also standardizes a UserInfo endpoint and discovery metadata.
s1_definition.analogy: Plain OAuth2 gives a partner app a pass that says what it may do with Rajesh's data, but it never officially says who Rajesh is. OIDC adds an official identity certificate — the ID token — stamped by National Bank of India, that states "this is Rajesh Kumar, email rajesh@example.com, verified by us." Now the partner site not only has permission to read data, it also knows, with the bank's signature, exactly which customer just logged in. OIDC is OAuth2 plus a trustworthy name tag.
s1_definition.oneliner: OAuth2 answers what the app may do; OIDC adds a signed ID token that answers who the user is.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer built on top of OAuth2 that adds standardized authentication — telling the client who the user is — whereas plain OAuth2 only handles authorization. OIDC introduces the ID token, a signed JWT containing identity claims such as sub, name, email, and picture, issued by the Authorization Server (acting as an OpenID Provider). The client validates the ID token to establish the user's identity, while still receiving an OAuth2 access token for calling APIs. OIDC also standardizes a UserInfo endpoint and discovery metadata.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Plain OAuth2 gives a partner app a pass that says what it may do with Rajesh's data, but it never officially says who Rajesh is. OIDC adds an official identity certificate — the ID token — stamped by National Bank of India, that states "this is Rajesh Kumar, email rajesh@example.com, verified by us." Now the partner site not only has permission to read data, it also knows, with the bank's signature, exactly which customer just logged in. OIDC is OAuth2 plus a trustworthy name tag.

**One line to remember:** OAuth2 answers what the app may do; OIDC adds a signed ID token that answers who the user is.

sections.s2_technical:
OIDC reuses the OAuth2 Authorization Code flow but adds the openid scope: `scope=openid profile email`. The Authorization Server, now an OpenID Provider, returns not only an access token but also an id_token, which is a JWT with identity claims. Standard claims include sub (a stable user identifier), iss (issuer), aud (the client id), exp/iat (timing), and profile claims like name, email, and picture. For example, after login the client decodes the id_token and reads `claims.get("email")` to greet the user.

The client must validate the ID token before trusting it: verify the signature with the provider's public key (fetched from the JWKS endpoint), check iss equals the expected provider, check aud equals its own client id, and check exp. A nonce sent in the auth request and echoed in the id_token prevents replay. The provider also exposes a discovery document at `/.well-known/openid-configuration` listing endpoints and keys, and a UserInfo endpoint that returns additional claims when called with the access token.

The senior distinction is crucial: the access token is for calling resource APIs and is opaque to the client's business logic, while the id_token is for the client itself to learn the user's identity and must never be sent to resource servers as an API credential. Login with Google, Microsoft, and Okta are all OIDC. The practical benefit is single sign-on and delegated identity: the bank authenticates the user once and many relying applications trust the signed ID token instead of each building their own password system.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A partner wealth-management site wants customers to sign in with their National Bank of India identity and wants to display the customer's name and email on the dashboard. Plain OAuth2 gives a token to call APIs but does not officially tell the site who logged in. This is exactly what OIDC adds — a signed ID token carrying identity.

Problem 2 — The site must be certain the identity claim really came from the bank and was not forged or replayed. This is exactly why the ID token is a validated JWT with issuer, audience, expiry, and nonce checks.

Our mini-project builds an `OpenIdProvider` that issues an id_token (plus access token) and a `RelyingParty` that validates the id_token and extracts identity. The demo shows a successful login and identity extraction, a rejected id_token with the wrong audience, and a rejected replay with a mismatched nonce.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: subject rajesh-001, client wealth-site, and a random nonce.

Step 1: The relying party sends the user to the OpenID Provider with the openid scope and a nonce. The provider authenticates the user and issues an ID token with claims including iss, sub, aud equal to wealth-site, the nonce, name, and email, plus the access token.

Step 2: The relying party validates the ID token: signature valid, issuer matches, audience equals its own client id, and nonce matches what it sent. All pass, so it trusts the identity and greets "Rajesh Kumar rajesh@example.com." Now the site knows who logged in, with the bank's signature.

Step 3: A tampered token addressed to other-site is presented. The audience check fails because aud is not wealth-site, so the relying party rejects it — this stops a token minted for another app being replayed here.

Step 4: The original token is replayed with a different expected nonce. The nonce check fails, so it is rejected as a possible replay. These checks are exactly why the ID token is a validated JWT rather than a plain claim.

```text
2026-10-31 23:30:00.010 INFO    [OidcLoginDemo] Provider issued ID token for sub=rajesh-001
2026-10-31 23:30:00.012 INFO    [OidcLoginDemo] Logged in as: Rajesh Kumar <rajesh@example.com>
2026-10-31 23:30:00.013 SEVERE  [OidcLoginDemo] Rejected ID token (wrong audience): audience mismatch: other-site
2026-10-31 23:30:00.014 WARNING [OidcLoginDemo] Rejected replay (nonce mismatch): nonce mismatch (possible replay)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Browser(Rajesh)      Relying Party(wealth-site)      OpenID Provider(bank)
      │                        │                               │
      │ click "Login with Bank"│  authorize?scope=openid&nonce │
      │────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ authenticate
      │◀──── code ──────────────────────────────────────────────│
      │                        │ exchange code ────────────────▶│
      │                        │◀── access_token + id_token ────│
      │                        │ validate id_token:             │
      │                        │  sig/iss/aud/exp/nonce        │
      │◀── "Welcome Rajesh" ───│ identity = {sub,name,email}    │
  access_token → used for API calls ; id_token → identity ONLY (never to APIs)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — OIDC Single Sign-On ═══

  ┌──────────────┐  OIDC (openid scope) ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ Relying Party│─────────────────────▶│ OpenID Provider     │ id_token + access
  │ (wealth-site)│◀────id_token+access──│ (bank, JWKS,UserInfo)│
  └──────┬───────┘ validate id_token    └─────────────────────┘
         │ access_token
         ▼
  ┌─────────────────────┐  JWKS /.well-known/openid-configuration
  │ Resource Server     │  discovery + public keys
  │ (bank APIs)         │
  └─────────────────────┘
  Many apps trust one provider → SSO, no per-app passwords
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — OIDC provider + relying party ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │     OpenIdProvider       │        │       RelyingParty        │
  │ ──────────────────────── │        │ ───────────────────────── │
  │ + issueIdToken(sub,aud,  │───────▶│ + login(idToken, nonce):  │
  │     nonce): claims        │id_token│     identity              │
  └──────────────────────────┘        │   throws IdTokenValidation│
                                       └───────────────────────────┘
  ID token claims: iss, sub, aud, exp, iat, nonce, name, email, picture

  Validation order in login():
    1. signature (JWKS public key)
    2. iss == expected provider
    3. aud == own client_id
    4. exp not passed
    5. nonce == sent nonce (replay protection)

  Rule: id_token = identity for the CLIENT; access_token = API credential.
  Never send id_token to resource servers as an API token.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
OpenID Connect is an identity layer built on top of OAuth2 that adds standardized authentication, meaning it tells the client who the user is, which plain OAuth2 does not do. OIDC introduces the ID token, a signed JWT containing identity claims such as sub, name, email, and picture, issued by the Authorization Server acting as an OpenID Provider. The client still receives an OAuth2 access token for calling APIs, but now it also gets a trustworthy, signed statement of the user's identity.

In my banking project a partner wealth-management site lets customers sign in with their National Bank of India identity and shows their name and email on the dashboard. We add the openid scope to the Authorization Code flow, and the provider returns an id_token alongside the access token. The site decodes the id_token to learn who logged in, so it never has to build or store passwords itself.

The validation is where I show rigor. Before trusting the ID token the relying party verifies the signature with the provider's public key from the JWKS endpoint, checks the issuer, checks that the audience equals its own client id, checks expiry, and checks that the nonce matches the one it sent to prevent replay. In my demo a good token logs the user in, a token addressed to another audience is rejected, and a replay with a mismatched nonce is rejected.

The distinction I always stress is that the access token is for calling resource APIs while the ID token is only for the client to learn the user's identity, and the ID token must never be sent to resource servers as an API credential. Login with Google, Microsoft, and Okta are all OIDC, and the big payoff for a bank is single sign-on with delegated identity: the bank authenticates once and many relying applications trust the signed ID token.

---

keyPoints: OAuth2: delegated authorization — app accesses user data on their behalf
Authorization Code Flow: safest for web apps — code exchanged server-to-server
PKCE: extra security for mobile/SPA — no client secret needed
OIDC: authentication layer on top of OAuth2 — ID token with user info
